rows.stem: If \(A = [a_{ij}] = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 5 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(c_{ij}\) is the cofactor of element \(a_{ij}\), then the value of \(a_{21} \cdot c_{11} + a_{22} \cdot c_{12} + a_{23} \cdot c_{13}\) is :
rows.solution: The expression pairs the elements of the SECOND row with the cofactors of the FIRST row, and such a mismatched expansion is always zero. Checking directly, \(c_{11} = +\begin{vmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 12\), \(c_{12} = -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 5 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = -(4 - 10) = 6\) and \(c_{13} = +\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 5 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -15\), while \(a_{21} = 1\), \(a_{22} = 3\), \(a_{23} = 2\). Hence \(a_{21}c_{11} + a_{22}c_{12} + a_{23}c_{13} = 1(12) + 3(6) + 2(-15) = 12 + 18 - 30 = 0\). (The reason it vanishes is that this sum is the determinant of the matrix obtained by copying row 2 over row 1, which then has two equal rows.)

rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A^2 - kA - 5I = O\), then the value of k is :
rows.solution: First compute \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 15 \\ 15 & 25 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(A^2 - kA - 5I = \begin{bmatrix} 10 - k - 5 & 15 - 3k \\ 15 - 3k & 25 - 4k - 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 - k & 15 - 3k \\ 15 - 3k & 20 - 4k \end{bmatrix}\). For this to be the null matrix every entry must vanish, and all three conditions \(5 - k = 0\), \(15 - 3k = 0\) and \(20 - 4k = 0\) agree on \(k = 5\).

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.solution: Taking logarithms turns the exponential into something easy to differentiate: \(e^{x^2 y} = c\) gives \(x^2 y = \log c\), a constant. Differentiating with respect to \(x\) by the product rule, \(2xy + x^2 \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{2xy}{x^2} = \dfrac{-2y}{x}\).

rows.stem: The value of constant c that makes the function f defined by \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 - c^2, & \text{if } x < 4 \\ cx + 20, & \text{if } x \geq 4 \end{cases}\) continuous for all real numbers is :
rows.solution: Each piece is a polynomial, so the only place continuity can fail is the join at \(x = 4\). There the left-hand limit is \(\lim\limits_{x \to 4^-}(x^2 - c^2) = 16 - c^2\), while the right-hand limit and the value are both \(4c + 20\). Equating, \(16 - c^2 = 4c + 20\), so \(c^2 + 4c + 4 = 0\), that is \((c + 2)^2 = 0\). Hence \(c = -2\), a repeated root, so this is the only value that works.

rows.subtopic: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem
rows.solution: The integrand \(|x|\) is an even function, so \(\int\limits_{-1}^{1}|x|\, dx = 2\int\limits_{0}^{1}|x|\, dx\), and on \([0, 1]\) we have \(|x| = x\). Hence the value is \(2\int\limits_{0}^{1} x\, dx = 2\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\). (A negative value is impossible in any case, since \(|x| \ge 0\) throughout.)

rows.stem: The number of arbitrary constants in the particular solution of the differential equation \(\log\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) = 3x + 4y;\ y(0) = 0\) is/are
rows.solution: This is a definition question rather than a calculation. The general solution of a first-order differential equation carries one arbitrary constant; a PARTICULAR solution is what is left once that constant has been pinned down by the given condition, here \(y(0) = 0\). A particular solution therefore contains no arbitrary constant at all, so the number is \(0\). (For the record, separating variables in \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{3x + 4y}\) gives \(-\dfrac{1}{4}e^{-4y} = \dfrac{1}{3}e^{3x} + C\), and \(y(0) = 0\) fixes \(C = -\dfrac{7}{12}\), leaving nothing arbitrary.)

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: A vector perpendicular to the line \(\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k} + \lambda(3\hat{i} - \hat{j})\) is :
rows.solution: A vector is perpendicular to the line exactly when it is perpendicular to the line's direction vector \(\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j}\), that is, when its scalar product with \(\vec{b}\) is zero. Testing the four choices: \((5\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 6\hat{k}) \cdot \vec{b} = 15 - 1 = 14\); \((\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}) \cdot \vec{b} = 3 - 3 = 0\); \((2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j}) \cdot \vec{b} = 6 + 2 = 8\); and \((9\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}) \cdot \vec{b} = 27 + 3 = 30\) — indeed \(9\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} = 3\vec{b}\) is parallel to the line, not perpendicular to it. Only \(\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}\) gives zero, so that is the required vector.

rows.stem: Show that \(f(x) = \dfrac{4 \sin x}{2 + \cos x} - x\) is an increasing function of \(x\) in \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
rows.solution: Differentiate by the quotient rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{4\sin x}{2 + \cos x}\right) = \dfrac{4\cos x(2 + \cos x) - 4\sin x(-\sin x)}{(2 + \cos x)^2} = \dfrac{8\cos x + 4\cos^2 x + 4\sin^2 x}{(2 + \cos x)^2} = \dfrac{8\cos x + 4}{(2 + \cos x)^2}\). Hence \(f'(x) = \dfrac{8\cos x + 4}{(2 + \cos x)^2} - 1 = \dfrac{8\cos x + 4 - (4 + 4\cos x + \cos^2 x)}{(2 + \cos x)^2} = \dfrac{4\cos x - \cos^2 x}{(2 + \cos x)^2} = \dfrac{\cos x\,(4 - \cos x)}{(2 + \cos x)^2}\). Now on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) we have \(\cos x \ge 0\); also \(\cos x \le 1\) so \(4 - \cos x > 0\), and the denominator is a square and hence positive. Therefore \(f'(x) \ge 0\) throughout \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), which shows that \(f\) is an increasing function there.

[CBSE marking scheme: the scheme reproduces this question with the logarithm inverted, as \(\log\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right)\); the question paper prints \(\log\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\), as above. Nothing turns on it — the two integrands are negatives of each other and both are odd, so either way the value is \(0\), by the scheme's own argument.] The interval \(\left[-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right]\) is symmetric about the origin, so test the integrand for oddness. Let \(f(x) = \cos x \cdot \log\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\). Then \(f(-x) = \cos(-x) \cdot \log\left(\dfrac{1-x}{1+x}\right) = \cos x \cdot \left[-\log\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\right] = -f(x)\), using \(\cos(-x) = \cos x\) and \(\log\dfrac{1}{t} = -\log t\). So \(f\) is an odd function, and the integral of an odd function over an interval symmetric about the origin is zero. Hence \(\int\limits_{-1/2}^{1/2} \cos x \cdot \log\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right) dx = 0\).

rows.stem: Given that \(x^{y} + y^{x} = a^{b}\), where a and b are positive constants, find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).
rows.solution:
Neither term can be differentiated directly, since each has a variable in both base and exponent, so treat them separately by logarithmic differentiation. Put \(u = x^y\) and \(v = y^x\), so that \(u + v = a^b\), a constant.
For \(u = x^y\): \(\log u = y\log x\), and differentiating, \(\dfrac{1}{u}\dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x} + \log x \dfrac{dy}{dx}\), so \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = x^y\left(\dfrac{y}{x} + \log x \dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)\).
For \(v = y^x\): \(\log v = x\log y\), and differentiating, \(\dfrac{1}{v}\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{x}{y}\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \log y\), so \(\dfrac{dv}{dx} = y^x\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \log y\right)\).
Since \(u + v\) is constant, \(\dfrac{du}{dx} + \dfrac{dv}{dx} = 0\), giving \(x^{y-1}y + x^y \log x \dfrac{dy}{dx} + y^{x-1}x \dfrac{dy}{dx} + y^x \log y = 0\). Collecting the \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) terms, \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{-\left(x^{y-1}y + y^x \log y\right)}{x^y \log x + y^{x-1}x}\).

Rather than set up three unknowns, split the numerator to match the factors: \(2x + 3 = (x + 3) + x\). Then \(I = \int \dfrac{x + 3}{x^2(x + 3)}\, dx + \int \dfrac{x}{x^2(x + 3)}\, dx = \int \dfrac{dx}{x^2} + \int \dfrac{dx}{x(x + 3)}\). For the second integral use the same trick again: \(\dfrac{1}{x(x + 3)} = \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{(x + 3) - x}{x(x + 3)} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{1}{x + 3}\right)\). Hence \(I = \int \dfrac{dx}{x^2} + \dfrac{1}{3}\int \dfrac{dx}{x} - \dfrac{1}{3}\int \dfrac{dx}{x + 3} = -\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{1}{3}\log|x| - \dfrac{1}{3}\log|x + 3| + c\). (Check at \(x = 1\): the derivative is \(\dfrac{1}{x^2} + \dfrac{1}{3x} - \dfrac{1}{3(x + 3)} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{5}{4}\), which is the integrand \(\dfrac{2 + 3}{1 \times 4}\).)

rows.subtopic: Graphical Solution and the Feasible Region
rows.stem:
Solve the following L.P.P. graphically :

Maximise \(Z = x + 3y\)

subject to the constraints :

\(x + 2y \le 200\)

\(x + y \le 150\)

\(y \le 75\)

\(x, y \ge 0\)
rows.solution: [CBSE marking scheme: the question REPRODUCED at the head of this item in the scheme is a different linear programming problem altogether — it prints 'Maximise \(Z = 2x + 3y\) subject to \(x + y \le 6\), \(x \ge 2\), \(y \le 3\)'. That is not the question on the paper. The scheme's own SOLUTION, however, plots \(x + 2y \le 200\), \(x + y \le 150\), \(y \le 75\) and maximises \(Z = x + 3y\), which is the printed question, and it is correct; only the restated question block is wrong.] Draw \(x + 2y = 200\), \(x + y = 150\) and \(y = 75\) in the first quadrant. The feasible region is the part of the first quadrant on or below all three lines, and it is bounded. Its corner points are: \(E(0, 0)\); \(A(0, 75)\), where \(y = 75\) meets the \(y\)-axis; \(B(50, 75)\), where \(y = 75\) meets \(x + 2y = 200\), since then \(x = 200 - 150 = 50\); \(C(100, 50)\), where \(x + 2y = 200\) meets \(x + y = 150\), since subtracting gives \(y = 50\) and then \(x = 100\); and \(D(150, 0)\), where \(x + y = 150\) meets the \(x\)-axis. Evaluating \(Z = x + 3y\): at \(A(0, 75)\), \(Z = 225\); at \(B(50, 75)\), \(Z = 50 + 225 = 275\); at \(C(100, 50)\), \(Z = 100 + 150 = 250\); at \(D(150, 0)\), \(Z = 150\); at \(E(0, 0)\), \(Z = 0\). The region is bounded, so the greatest of these is the maximum. Hence \(Z\) is maximum and equal to \(275\) at \(x = 50\), \(y = 75\).

rows.stem:
Use the product of matrices \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -7 & 7 & -7 \\ -7 & 5 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\) to solve the following system of equations :

\(x + 2y - 3z = 6\)

\(3x + 2y - 2z = 3\)

\(2x - y + z = 2\)
rows.solution:
Call the two given matrices \(A\) and \(B\). Multiplying them out, \(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -7 & 7 & -7 \\ -7 & 5 & -4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = 7I\). (For instance the first entry is \(1(0) + 2(-7) + (-3)(-7) = 7\) and the next is \(1(1) + 2(7) + (-3)(5) = 0\).) Since \(AB = 7I\), we get \(A\left(\dfrac{1}{7}B\right) = I\), so \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{7}B\).
The system is exactly \(AX = C\) with \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}\) and \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), because the coefficient matrix of the three equations is \(A\). Hence \(X = A^{-1}C = \dfrac{1}{7}BC = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 \\ -7 & 7 & -7 \\ -7 & 5 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ -35 \\ -35 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix}\). Therefore \(x = 1\), \(y = -5\), \(z = -5\), which checks in all three equations: \(1 - 10 + 15 = 6\), \(3 - 10 + 10 = 3\) and \(2 + 5 - 5 = 2\).
